Ghee is a type of pure, clarified fat made from butter — most commonly cow's butter — that has been slowly cooked until all its water has evaporated and all its milk solids have been removed. What remains is nearly 100% pure butterfat: a rich, golden, highly shelf-stable cooking fat.
The simplest way to picture it

Start with regular butter. Butter is not pure fat — it contains water (about 15–17%) and milk proteins and sugars (about 3–5%). When you melt butter in a pan on low heat and keep it going long enough, three things happen: the water boils away as steam, and the milk proteins and sugars sink to the bottom and gently toast or float to the top as foam. You skim or strain those solids away, and what you're left with — that clear, golden liquid — is ghee. It is butter, stripped down to its purest form.
What it looks, smells, and tastes like

• Color: Deep golden-yellow, sometimes amber. The longer it is cooked, the deeper the color.
  • Texture: At room temperature (below roughly 25°C / 77°F), ghee is semi-solid or fully solid, like soft wax or thick coconut oil. When warm, it is a clear, flowing liquid.
  • Smell: Distinctly nutty, warm, and rich — noticeably more flavorful than plain melted butter. This nutty aroma comes from the milk solids having gently browned before being removed, a process very similar to making "brown butter."
  • Taste: Deep, buttery, slightly caramel-like, and richer than ordinary butter. It coats the palate in a way that feels luxurious.
How ghee differs from regular butter and plain clarified butter

These three things are related but distinct:

Regular butter contains fat, water, and milk solids all together. Because of the water and proteins, it burns easily when heated, foams in the pan, and spoils relatively quickly.

Clarified butter is butter that has been melted and had its water and milk solids removed — similar to ghee, but the process stops earlier. It is cooked just long enough to separate the components, without letting the milk solids toast or brown at all.

Ghee goes one step further than clarified butter. It is cooked slowly and long enough that any remaining moisture is completely gone and the milk solids are allowed to brown slightly before being removed. This extra step is what gives ghee its distinctly deeper, nuttier flavor — and what makes it even more shelf-stable than clarified butter.

Think of it this way: clarified butter and ghee are made by the same method, but ghee is the more fully reduced, more flavorful, more traditional version of the two.
Where ghee comes from and its cultural importance

Ghee is deeply rooted in South Asian culture, particularly in India, where it has been made and used for thousands of years. It is a staple ingredient across Indian, Pakistani, Bangladeshi, Nepali, and Sri Lankan cooking. It also appears prominently in Middle Eastern and some Southeast Asian cuisines.

In India, ghee is not just food — it carries enormous cultural, religious, and symbolic significance. In Hinduism, it is considered sacred and pure. It is used in religious ceremonies, offered into sacred fires during rituals (havan or yagna), and used to light oil lamps in temples and homes. It is also a central ingredient in Ayurveda, the ancient Indian system of medicine, where it is regarded as deeply nourishing and healing — believed to aid digestion, strengthen the body, and support overall health.

In many South Asian households, homemade ghee — simmered slowly from cultured butter or cream — is a matter of household pride and tradition.
How ghee is used in cooking

Ghee is an extremely versatile cooking fat. Its most practical advantage over butter is its very high smoke point — around 250°C (480°F), compared to regular butter's 150°C (300°F). This means you can use ghee for high-heat cooking like deep-frying, sautéing, and searing without it burning or smoking, something butter simply cannot do.

Some common uses:

  • As a cooking fat for frying spices, onions, and aromatics at the start of curries and dals — the heat releases the flavor of the spices directly into the ghee, which then carries those flavors throughout the dish.
  • For making rice dishes like biryani and pulao, where ghee is mixed in for richness and flavor.
  • Drizzled over finished dishes — a small spoonful of ghee poured over hot dal (lentil soup), rice, khichdi, or roti just before eating adds enormous flavor and richness.
  • In baking and sweets — ghee is essential in Indian sweets (mithai) like halwa, ladoo, and mysore pak, giving them their characteristic richness.
  • Spread on flatbreads — rotis, parathas, and naans are often finished with a brush of ghee right off the heat.
  • As a finishing fat in many global cuisines, drizzled over vegetables, meats, or soups for flavor.

Because ghee has no water and no milk solids, it does not spoil the way butter does. It is highly resistant to bacterial growth and rancidity. Properly made ghee stored in a clean, dry, airtight container can last:

  • At room temperature: Several weeks to a few months.
  • In the refrigerator: Up to a year or more.
  • In the freezer: Indefinitely.

A critical rule: always use a dry spoon to scoop ghee. Even a small drop of water introduced into the jar can cause it to spoil much faster.

Ghee is almost entirely saturated fat, since it is pure butterfat. It contains fat-soluble vitamins — A, D, E, and K — which are retained from the original butter. Because the milk solids (which contain lactose and casein, the milk sugar and milk protein) are removed during the making of ghee, people who are lactose intolerant or sensitive to dairy proteins often find they can tolerate ghee even when they cannot tolerate butter or other dairy products. However, it is important to note that ghee is a calorie-dense fat, and how much of it is healthy to consume depends entirely on the overall context of a person's diet.

Ghee is butter cooked down to its purest fat form — water gone, milk solids removed — leaving a golden, nutty, shelf-stable cooking fat with a deep flavor, a very high smoke point, and enormous cultural significance across South Asia. It is at once a practical kitchen staple, a sacred ritual ingredient, and a centuries-old symbol of nourishment and purity.
